dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Exhaustively read reference source: app.rb, every model, all 14 migrations individually, markdown/liquid setup, seeds, helpers — full structural enumeration, exceeding a skim.

Read all middleware (csp, rate_limit, etag, conditional_get, csrf_double_submit, audit, compression, cors, timing), all job handlers incl. runner.rb, and read jobs migration 009 + job.rb (claim/queue source); grepped routes and read app.rb route bodies in full slices.
Read spec_helper.rb and job files to understand expected behavior — but only source; never ran or curled the reference to empirically confirm status/headers/ETag/CSP/link formats.

Entire debugging/verification tail tests only the agent's own Rust server; no reference probing, no revisiting reference to resolve mismatches. Orientation was front-loaded, not sustained; no durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables) was built.
No evidence of enumerating RJ_* env vars (no ENV grep) and no empirical reference probing anywhere in the trajectory — the live-probing half of the dimension is absent.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's source-based orientation is very thorough — it read essentially every reference file (routes, models, all migrations, middleware, jobs, specs), exceeding anchor 5's 'major files' bar and grasping the jobs schema and claim source. However, it never once ran or curled the reference to empirically confirm behavior, never enumerated RJ_* vars explicitly, built no durable behavioral model, and did all verification against its own server with orientation entirely front-loaded. The absent live-probing and sustained re-orientation keep it below anchor 8; the exhaustive source read plus jobs-schema understanding place it squarely at 5.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Agent states an ordered subsystem plan: update Cargo.toml → database layer → routes/middleware/templates → start.sh, and 'build incrementally, starting with the database schema and health endpoint, then adding...' — an explicit sensible ordering (DB/health before features).

Repeated enumerated subsystem list (accounts, sessions, posts, comments, tags, search, notifications, media, feeds, admin, HTML pages, jobs) shows a real decomposition, but the same list is restated many times without per-piece completion criteria.

Milestone-ish intent to get minimal /_health compiling then 'append remaining route handlers in batches, rebuilding after each batch to catch errors early' — the only concrete done-signal used is 'does it compile,' not a parity check against the reference.

Middle of the run collapses into undifferentiated compile-error and file-corruption firefighting across a monolithic main.rs; the stated incremental milestone discipline is largely abandoned, and risky shared-state pieces (job-queue claim semantics/BEGIN IMMEDIATE, CSRF, header contracts) are never singled out or sequenced early.

Only near the very end does ad-hoc endpoint testing appear (account create, login, post CRUD, RSS, 404) — a rough functional done-check applied to the whole app at once, not a per-milestone parity exit test.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent has an explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order (reference read → skeleton → DB → health → handlers → jobs/admin) and a rough done-signal, which clears anchor 3's 'vague mental list.' But the done-signals are weak — mostly 'it compiles' plus a single batch of ad-hoc endpoint tests at the end — rather than a concrete parity check per milestone, and the foundational/risky shared-state interfaces (jobs claim semantics, CSRF, header contracts) are never tiered by risk or sequenced first, which anchor 8 requires. The middle of the trajectory degrades into a monolithic build with reactive error-fixing, so the milestone structure isn't sustained. That places it between 3 and 5, landing at 4.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Verification consists of starting its own binary and hitting /_health plus a few routes with curl, checking responses 'are correct' by eye. No comparison to the reference server.

Ran a python integration script exercising a CRUD flow (account, login, post, feeds, admin) against its own server; caught its own bugs (markdown excerpt, home-page link entities, only-first-tag-assigned) by visually inspecting output — no normalization, no reference diff.

Final 'verification' just re-runs the same self-tests (health, account, login, post, RSS, 404) and declares parity; no differential harness, no dynamic-key elision/HTML-whitespace/header-set normalization, and no cross-runtime job-queue test against the real reference.

The Ruby reference was extensively read as source but never executed; across the whole trajectory there is no instance of running the reference server to compare responses, confirming verification never became differential.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent only ran a handful of curl/python requests against its own service and eyeballed whether the JSON/HTML looked plausible, catching a few self-inflicted bugs in the process — matching anchor 3 ('runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse'). It never scripted side-by-side requests to both servers or diffed against the reference (anchor 5), built no normalizing differential harness (anchor 8), and never exercised the cross-runtime job queue, ETag/rate-limit headers, or hard constraints as parity checks. It sits slightly above anchor 0 because it did test multiple subsystems in an integration script, but well short of anchor 5 since no reference comparison ever occurred.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: During the long read phase, 'progress' is tracked entirely as which reference FILES remain to read (repeated 'still need migrations, middleware, jobs...'), never as which subsystems match the reference. No parity coverage tracking exists.

In the build phase, tracking is 'which route handlers remain to append' — a build/sequencing to-do, not a done-vs-remaining parity ledger. No harness comparing against the reference is ever built or run.

End smoke test finds 3 real bugs (markdown excerpt, HTML entity links, only-first-tag-assigned) but dismisses them as 'minor issues' and moves toward declaring completion — no accounting of which subsystems actually pass.

Declares the port 'functionally complete' and lists every subsystem (rate-limit, CSRF, ETag, job queue, media, feeds) as working based on ~8 manual curls, none compared to the reference. Classic 'declare done based on the last thing touched' with no passing/failing/not-attempted distinction.

The only regression-like awareness is self-inflicted compile breakage while editing (list_notifications signature deleted), not detection that a change regressed a previously-passing subsystem — confirming no baseline/regression guard for parity.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintains only a vague, prose-level recollection of what it built and enumerates subsystems from the reference, but never establishes any harness-backed coverage ledger, never runs the reference for comparison, and has no passing/failing/not-yet-attempted distinction. It declares the port 'complete' based on a few self-authored smoke tests and the last code touched, even dismissing freshly-found bugs as 'minor,' with no guard against regressions in shared code. This matches anchor 3 ('vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code'), above 0 only because it does keep a mental list of subsystems and remaining handlers, but well short of anchor 5's running parity checklist.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: Agent reverse-engineers the reference by reading files, then commits to an implementation. It never runs the Ruby reference or sets up any response comparison, so no parity divergence can ever be surfaced to trigger course-correction.

Genuine root-cause approach change (shell heredocs -> Python generator) after recurring file corruption. Shows adaptive capability, but it is about code-authoring tooling, not about reference-behavior parity, so it does not exercise this dimension.
Fixes a runtime panic (UUID slice [..48] on 32-char string) — an implementation bug found by exercising its own server, not a reference-parity mismatch or assumption revision.

Testing its own output reveals rendering bugs (HTML remnants in excerpts, entity-escaped links, only first tag assigned). Agent patches them locally and labels them 'minor', never re-deriving correct behavior from the reference nor re-verifying the affected subsystem against it.

Submits as complete based solely on its own integration smoke tests ('all integration tests passed'), with no comparison to reference behavior — barreling ahead on read-derived assumptions that were never validated.

dimensions.reasoning: Because the agent never built or used any comparison against the running reference, parity divergences were never detected, so the dimension is almost unexercised: it barrels ahead on read-only assumptions (anchor 0 territory). The small amount of correction present (steps 125, 128) is local fixing of self-observed implementation/rendering bugs without questioning underlying assumptions about reference behavior or re-verifying against the reference, matching the lower half of anchor 3. Averaging these — near-absent parity-driven correction plus a little local, non-parity bug fixing — places the observed level at 2.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Chose native Rust crates (axum, rusqlite bundled, bcrypt, comrak) and read runner.rb; the port is a genuine Rust service, structurally avoiding the Ruby-bridge/proxy risk. But there is no explicit audit of Cargo.toml against the prohibited crate list, nor any process-tree/no-TCP check.

Binary size checked repeatedly via `ls -la target/release` and `du -h`, each time explicitly noting '~6.3-6.4MB, well under 40MB cap'. This is the one hard constraint actively and repeatedly verified.

Read the reference runner.rb to understand job semantics, but there is no evidence the agent treated BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter semantics as a matched contract or tested cross-runtime interop against the live reference.

Final verification loop tested functional endpoints (/_health, CRUD, feeds) but never measured /_health latency ratio vs Ruby, never audited the running process tree for Ruby runtimes, and never exercised the shared-DB job-queue interop — none of these constraints were baked into a standing gate.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept the binary-size cap firmly in mind and verified it multiple times, and by choosing native Rust crates it structurally satisfied the no-Ruby-bridge/no-proxy rules — matching anchor 5's 'verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary under cap).' It falls short of anchor 8 because it never actively guarded the other hard constraints: no process-tree/no-TCP audit, no latency-parity measurement, and no verification that shared-DB BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter semantics matched the reference. So its observed behavior sits at 5, not higher.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
